## Problem 2

### Accelerometers have become an appealing alternative to self-report techniques for studying physical activity in observational studies and clinical trials, largely because of their relative objectivity. During observation periods, the devices can measure MIMS in a short period; one-minute intervals are common. Because accelerometers can be worn comfortably and unobtrusively, they produce around-the-clock observations.

### This problem uses accelerometer data collected on 250 participants in the NHANES study. The participants’ demographic data can be downloaded here, and their accelerometer data can be downloaded here. Variables *MIMS are the MIMS values for each minute of a 24-hour day starting at midnight.

### Load, tidy, merge, and otherwise organize the data sets. Your final dataset should include all originally observed variables; exclude participants less than 21 years of age, and those with missing demographic data; and encode data with reasonable variable classes (i.e. not numeric, and using factors with the ordering of tables and plots in mind).

#### Load Data
```{r}
nhanes_accel_df <- read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")
nhanes_covar_df <- read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)
```
#### Tidy the acceleration data:
```{r}
nhanes_accel_df = nhanes_accel_df |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(contains("min"),
               names_to = "min",
               values_to = "accel",
               names_prefix = "min") |> 
  mutate(min = as.numeric(min))
```

#### Tidy covariates:
```{r}
nhanes_covar_df = nhanes_covar_df |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> ## Clean the names.
  mutate(sex = as.factor( ## Re-code factors and ordering.
    case_when(
      sex == 2 ~ "female",
      sex == 1 ~ "male"
    )
  ),
  education = factor(
    case_when(
      education == 1 ~ "less than hs",
      education == 2 ~ "hs equivalent",
      education == 3 ~ "more than hs"
    ), levels = c("less than hs", "hs equivalent", "more than hs")
  )) |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> ## Exclude participants less than 21 years old.
  drop_na() ## Remove NA values
```

#### Merge data:
```{r}
## Merge in participants keeping only those with full demographic data:
nhanes_df = nhanes_accel_df |> 
  right_join(nhanes_covar_df, by = "seqn") 
```


### Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category, and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category. Comment on these items.
```{r}
## Create the table:
nhanes_df |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = min, values_from = accel) |>
  group_by(education, sex) |> 
  summarize(n = n())

## Create the plot:
nhanes_df |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = min, values_from = accel) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, color = sex, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(. ~ education)
```

The table shows that there are fewer participants in the less than hs and the hs equivalent education groups relative to the more than hs education group. Also, the number of female and male participants are similar within the less than hs and more than hs groups, but there are much more male participants in the hs equivalent education group.

The plot shows interesting differences in the distribution of age across different levels of education and sex groups. We see that the participants with less than high school or high school equivalent education scores have more participants of higher age (except for males in the high school equivalent group, who are mostly younger). In contrast, participants with more than a high school education have a higher density of younger participants across both sexes.

### Traditional analyses of accelerometer data focus on the total activity over the day. Using your tidied data set, aggregate across minutes to create a total activity variable for each participant. Plot these total activities (y-axis) against age (x-axis); your plot should compare men to women and have separate panels for each education level. Include a trend line or a smooth to illustrate differences. Comment on your plot.
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  group_by(seqn, age, sex, education) |> 
  summarize(mean_accel = mean(accel)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = mean_accel, color = sex)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) +
  facet_wrap(. ~ education) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Mean Acceleration (Per Subject)",
       title = "Age vs Mean Activity Between Subjects",
       subtitle = "Seperated by Education Level and Sex") 
  
```
This plot shows a unique example of moderation based on level of education. Across the groups, activity (mean acceleration) decreases with increasing age. However, the relationship seems to become attenuated as education increases such that those of higher education have less of an decrease in activity as they age. We see some sex-related differences, with the largest intercept and rate differences between men and women seen in the higher education group.


### Accelerometer data allows the inspection activity over the course of the day. Make a three-panel plot that shows the 24-hour activity time courses for each education level and use color to indicate sex. Describe in words any patterns or conclusions you can make based on this graph; including smooth trends may help identify differences.
```{r}
## Plot data with points:
nhanes_df |> 
  group_by(min, sex, education) |> 
  summarize(mean_accel = mean(accel)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = min, y = mean_accel, color = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1)

## Plot only smoothed lines:
nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = min, y = accel, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1)
```

The curves show similar relationships across each education group with slight differences. We see across sex and education, that activity peaks in the waking hours of the day time and drops into the evening. Those with less than a high school degree seem to be more active earlier in the day with steeper decreases as the day progresses, while those with a high school diploma or above seem to have a more constant activity pattern during the day and then a sharper decline in the evening. The major sex differences are found in the group with a high school degree or above, as male participants seem to show less activity during the day.

I decided to interpret the question as asking for mean activity across each minute for each group. Otherwise, the points are far too overwhelming to gather meaningful data from the plot. I also included a plot with only the fitted spline equations to the original data to see where the underlying trends of activity show.
